card.official_title: AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
card.plain_title: Borrow $11.25 billion for affordable housing and veterans’ home loans
card.yes_means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to fund affordable housing programs and veterans’ home loans, repaying the money with interest over time.
card.no_means: Existing housing programs would continue without the additional $11.25 billion in borrowing authorized by this measure.

what_changes.today: The state uses bonds to fund some housing programs, repaying borrowed money with interest.
what_changes.if_passes: An additional $10 billion in housing bonds would be repaid from the General Fund, which pays for most state services.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: State grants and low-cost loans help fund housing generally reserved for low-income Californians.
what_changes.if_passes: The measure adds $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, generally reserving units for low-income households for 55 years.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: The state has used bonds to support homeownership programs.
what_changes.if_passes: The measure adds $1.1 billion for low- and moderate-income homeownership, including first-time buyer assistance and home repairs.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Public funds help pay for some housing construction; most homes are built entirely with private money.
what_changes.if_passes: The measure adds $1 billion for farmworker, student, and tribal housing, $500 million for infrastructure, and $200 million for local pilot projects.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Eligible veterans receive bond-funded home loans and repay the bonds through their loan payments.
what_changes.if_passes: An additional $1.25 billion in bonds would fund veterans’ home loans, with repayment through participating veterans’ payments.
what_changes.label: fact

who_is_affected: Low-income renters, including people who need housing with on-site support services
Low- and moderate-income homebuyers and low-income homeowners
Veterans eligible for state home loans
Farmworkers, tribal communities, and university students
State taxpayers and users of services funded by the General Fund

fiscal_impact.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates General Fund repayments of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years; veterans’ loan payments would cover the separate veterans’ bonds.
fiscal_impact.label: prediction

steelman_yes.headline: Supporters argue the added funding would build and preserve homes that veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, and working families can afford.
more_reasons: Supporters argue homebuyer assistance would expand access to homeownership, including for veterans.
Supporters argue preserving affordable housing would help people at risk of homelessness stay housed.

best_evidence.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates the funds would subsidize up to 40,000 multifamily rental units.
best_evidence.label: prediction

best_evidence.text: The measure provides $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans and $1.1 billion for other homeownership programs.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: Supporters emphasize veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, working families, and people at risk of homelessness.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: Supporters argue the investment would deliver needed homes without new taxes, bring in federal matching funds, and require public reporting on spending and results.

steelman_no.headline: No official argument against was submitted; a case against is that added borrowing would commit state funds to decades of repayments.
more_reasons: A further trade-off is that borrowing costs more than paying up front because the state must pay interest.

best_evidence.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates annual housing-bond repayments would equal about 0.25 percent of the General Fund budget.
best_evidence.label: prediction

best_evidence.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates borrowing would cost about 15 percent more than paying up front, after adjusting for inflation.
best_evidence.label: prediction

steelman_no.who_it_helps: This analysis-based case emphasizes taxpayers and people who rely on other General Fund services.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: The analysis-based reply is that additional housing assistance comes with long-term repayment obligations from the same account that funds education, health care, and other services.

crux.text: The main trade-off is additional housing assistance now versus long-term state debt and interest costs. No official opposition argument was submitted; the case against here reflects the budget trade-offs in the nonpartisan analysis.

evidence.text: Bond funding would be allocated over several years and much of it would be combined with other government money.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates homeownership programs would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans.
evidence.label: prediction

evidence.text: Veterans’ payments have always covered the bonds used for their home loans, with no direct state cost.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Some bond money would pay the increased costs of administering the housing programs.
evidence.label: fact

card.official_title: PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
card.plain_title: Make existing higher income tax rates permanent
card.yes_means: The existing higher income tax rates on the top 2 percent of California taxpayers would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
card.no_means: The existing higher income tax rates would remain temporary and expire in 2031.

what_changes.today: The higher income tax rates approved in 2012 and extended in 2016 expire in 2031.
what_changes.if_passes: Those higher rates would continue permanently.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: The state collects revenue from these higher rates, but they are scheduled to expire in 2031.
what_changes.if_passes: Keeping the rates would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion annually after their scheduled expiration.
what_changes.label: prediction

what_changes.today: About half of General Fund spending supports education, including universities, and about one-third supports health and human services.
what_changes.if_passes: Roughly 40 percent of the retained funding would support schools and community colleges, with the rest supporting other programs and reserves.
what_changes.label: prediction

who_is_affected: High-income taxpayers subject to the higher rates
Public school students, families and staff
Community college students and staff
People who rely on state-funded health care and other services

fiscal_impact.text: Making the rates permanent would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue after their scheduled expiration; the amount would vary widely with the stock market.
fiscal_impact.label: prediction

steelman_yes.headline: Supporters argue keeping this revenue would protect schools and health care from cuts when the higher tax rates expire.
more_reasons: Supporters argue it keeps current rates on only the top 2 percent of taxpayers rather than raising anyone’s current rate.
Supporters argue local spending decisions, annual audits and limits on administrative spending would protect classroom funding.

best_evidence.text: The measure would retain $5 billion to $15 billion annually, with roughly 40 percent of the funding going to schools and community colleges.
best_evidence.label: prediction

best_evidence.text: The existing higher rates apply to the top 2 percent of taxpayers.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: Supporters say students, school staff and families relying on Medi-Cal and other public services would benefit.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: Supporters argue the measure keeps rates unchanged today, while allowing them to expire would give high earners a tax cut and put public services at risk.

steelman_no.headline: Opponents argue keeping these taxes forever would deny taxpayers the lower rates promised when the temporary taxes were approved.
more_reasons: Opponents argue permanently higher income taxes would add to California’s cost of living.
Opponents argue the state should control waste and spending before committing to permanent tax revenue.

best_evidence.text: The measure removes the scheduled expiration of the higher income tax rates.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Opponents argue spending should be brought under control before higher taxes become permanent.
best_evidence.label: value
best_evidence.whose: Opponents in the official ballot argument

steelman_no.who_it_helps: Opponents say rejecting the measure would help taxpayers who would otherwise keep paying the higher rates and Californians concerned about spending and affordability.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: Opponents argue protecting services should start with better spending choices, rather than making temporary taxes permanent to sustain current spending.

crux.text: The choice is between retaining revenue for public services and allowing a scheduled tax reduction for high earners. The sides also disagree over whether service cuts would follow expiration or could be avoided through better spending choices.

evidence.text: The measure keeps existing rates rather than increasing them now, but taxpayers covered by those rates would pay more after 2030 than under current law.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: At 2025 income levels, the higher rates apply to income above about $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers; thresholds adjust annually for inflation.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.label: prediction

evidence.label: prediction

card.official_title: CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
card.plain_title: Change how state officials are replaced after a recall
card.yes_means: A yes vote removes the replacement contest from state recall ballots and fills recalled officials’ offices through succession, appointments or later elections.
card.no_means: A no vote keeps the same-ballot choice of whether to remove a state official and who should replace them, with the replacement receiving the most votes winning.

what_changes.today: Voters decide both whether to remove the official and who should replace them.
what_changes.if_passes: Voters decide only whether to remove the official.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: The replacement candidate with the most recall-election votes becomes Governor.
what_changes.if_passes: The Lieutenant Governor takes over until a statewide election if the recall occurs before the nomination deadline in the term’s first two years; otherwise, for the remaining term.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: The replacement is chosen in the same recall election.
what_changes.if_passes: The seat becomes vacant and typically is filled through a separate special election.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Voters choose a replacement in the recall election.
what_changes.if_passes: The Governor appoints replacements under existing vacancy rules.
what_changes.label: fact

who_is_affected: Voters deciding whether to recall state officials
State officials facing recall and potential replacement candidates
The Governor and Lieutenant Governor
State and county election offices and taxpayers

fiscal_impact.text: The net effect is unknown: state and local governments could save or spend millions of dollars on rare recall elections, depending on which offices are recalled and whether separate elections are needed.
fiscal_impact.label: prediction

steelman_yes.headline: Supporters argue it would prevent a replacement from winning a recall contest with only a small share of voters’ support.
more_reasons: Supporters argue removing the replacement contest would reduce incentives for costly recalls that simply repeat a recent election.
Supporters argue succession by the elected Lieutenant Governor would provide continuity after a Governor’s recall.

best_evidence.text: Under current rules, the replacement candidate with the most votes wins; a majority is not required.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Supporters argue separating removal from replacement would keep recalls focused on accountability rather than another contest for the office.
best_evidence.label: value
best_evidence.whose: Supporters in the official ballot argument

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: Voters who want to remove an official without allowing a replacement to win a crowded recall contest with limited support.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: Supporters reply that voters would retain the power to remove officials, while succession by an elected Lieutenant Governor and regular elections offer alternatives to a replacement winning with a small share of votes.

steelman_no.headline: Opponents argue it would take away voters’ same-election choice of a replacement and leave many replacements to appointment or succession.
more_reasons: Opponents argue separate replacement elections could leave seats vacant and add taxpayer costs.
Opponents argue allowing a recalled official to run in the later special election could undo the removal voters just approved.

best_evidence.text: The measure replaces same-ballot replacement contests with succession, appointments or separate elections, depending on the office.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: A recalled official may run in a special election to fill the office.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_no.who_it_helps: Voters who want to choose an immediate replacement themselves when removing a state official.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: Opponents reply that even a replacement chosen without a majority is chosen directly by voters; they value that choice over having an appointment or succession determine who takes office.

crux.text: Should voters choose a replacement in the recall election even if that candidate lacks majority support, or should succession, appointments and later elections replace that choice? The sides also disagree about whether the change would reduce costly recalls or add costs and delays.

evidence.text: The measure removes the replacement question, not voters’ decision about whether to remove an official.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Not every replacement would face a later special election: the Governor would appoint replacements for offices other than Governor and state legislative seats.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: After a later-term recall, the Lieutenant Governor would serve the rest of the Governor’s term.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Separate special elections could cost millions each, while shorter ballots without replacement candidates could save millions in other recalls; the net effect is unknown.
evidence.label: prediction

card.official_title: PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

card.no_means: A no vote would keep current spending-limit rules and existing audit practices without adding these requirements.

what_changes.today: The state has a constitutional tax-spending limit, with exclusions for spending such as infrastructure.

card.official_title: MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
card.plain_title: Change environmental review and lawsuit rules for eligible projects
card.yes_means: Eligible housing, transportation, water, health, and other project applicants could choose new environmental review and permit procedures with tighter deadlines and limits on review and court challenges.
card.no_means: Existing environmental review, permitting, and court challenge procedures would remain in place.

what_changes.today: Existing procedures have less binding time limits for environmental and permitting reviews.
what_changes.if_passes: Tighter deadlines apply, including a 365-business-day limit for environmental impact reports that applicants can seek to enforce.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: For detailed environmental reviews, agencies must develop and consider multiple alternatives that could reduce environmental harm.
what_changes.if_passes: Applicants may develop just one alternative for the agency to consider.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: State law sets minimum public review periods, not maximums.
what_changes.if_passes: Agencies face limits on how long they can accept public and other agencies’ comments.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Agencies must consult with a wider range of California native tribes than only federally recognized tribes.
what_changes.if_passes: Agencies and applicants need consult only with federally recognized California native tribes.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Courts can stop an entire project while an agency fixes a faulty environmental review.
what_changes.if_passes: Courts face decision deadlines and narrower review, and may stop only the part of a project with a faulty review.
what_changes.label: fact

who_is_affected: Applicants for eligible public and private projects
Residents near proposed projects and people who comment on or challenge them
California native tribes, including tribes without federal recognition
State and local agencies and courts
Taxpayers and people who would use new housing and infrastructure

fiscal_impact.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates initial state and local costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually, partly covered by fees. Longer-term effects could be larger, but whether they bring net costs or savings is uncertain.
fiscal_impact.label: prediction

best_evidence.text: The measure sets more binding deadlines for environmental review, permits, and court challenges.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: If the changes speed public construction, state and local project costs would likely fall.
best_evidence.label: prediction

steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: Supporters argue faster review need not sacrifice environmental protection: projects still undergo environmental review, and residents retain opportunities to comment, oppose projects, and sue.

best_evidence.text: Applicants may offer only one project alternative, replacing the requirement that agencies develop and consider multiple alternatives.

best_evidence.text: If changed procedures lead to environmental harm that otherwise would not occur, governments could face higher response costs.

steelman_no.who_it_helps: Opponents say keeping current rules protects nearby residents, people exposed to pollution, and taxpayers who might pay to address environmental damage.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: Opponents argue faster, cheaper construction does not ensure lower household bills, and that reduced review could create health and cleanup costs instead.

crux.text: The sides disagree about whether tighter timelines and narrower review would deliver meaningful household savings or create environmental and public costs. They also weigh faster construction against fuller public review and stronger court remedies differently.
